newsitem.title: USA: Forged letter traced, Miami bond firm owner says.
newsitem.headline: Forged letter traced, Miami bond firm owner says.

text.p: Miami bond firm owner Leo Guzman said a forged letter that resulted in his dismissal from a Dade County bond deal was sent by fax from the Miami home of a man whose family is involved in public finance.
Guzman said the information, obtained by subpoenaed phone company records, doesn't prove who faked the letter but at least proves the letter did not come from his office.
The letter was written on what appeared to be Guzman & Co letterhead, purportedly signed by Guzman, and faxed to Dade County officials and several news offices.
It accused one of Dade County's financial advisers, Rauscher Pierce Refsnes Inc, of violating a regulation against passing on certain municipal underwriting fees to issuers.

Rauscher Pierce denied the allegation and Guzman insisted he did not write the letter. But county commissioners booted Guzman's firm in December from a $430 million water sewer bond deal, saying that because of the letter "there is a shadow cast" on Guzman.
Guzman sued the county, and subpoenaed phone company records to learn who had faxed the letter to the Atlanta office of the Bond Buyer, a daily trade paper that covers municipal bonds, on Nov 27.
The Bond Buyer declined to comment, but said in Wednesay's editions that it agreed to give Guzman a copy of the fax.

Guzman's attorney matched the time on that copy of the fax with Bond Buyer phone records. He said the records indicated the letter was faxed from a Miami telephone number belonging to British Realty and Mortgage Corp.
According to state records, the phone with that number is at the home of the registered agent and principle for British Realty, M.L. Parekh.
Parekh did not return Reuter calls to the British Realty phone number. He has two sons active in the public finance arena.
One son, Dipak Parekh, budget director for the city of Miami, said, "I don't know anything about it."
Another son, Kishor Parekh, is a senior vice president at the Miami bond firm Howard Gary & Co. He could not be reached for comment.
Guzman said he still doesn't know who forged the letter or why, but that it clearly was written by "somebody who dispalyed a knowledge of the industry."
"It is clearly somebody who meant to do us harm and who in fact did us harm," Guzman said.

In his lawsuit against Dade County, Guzman alleged that he was dismissed from the Dade deal in part for ethnic reasons. Howard Gary & Co was dismissed from the same bond deal because of concerns about the role of company president Howard Gary as a government witness in a federal probe of public finance corruption.
Gary is black and in order to avoid the appearance of singling out his firm for racial reasons, the commission also dismissed the Hispanic-owned Guzman & Co, Guzman's lawsuit claims.
Guzman said the removal from the deal, which is to be priced Thursday, had cost his firm about $170,000 in fees.
"The damages to this firm vastly exceed the money lost in this transaction," Guzman said. "We have been substantially damaged in our reputation."
Guzman said he would continue to "follow this trail wherever it leads" and that if he learns who forged the letter, "We will absolutely pursue all of our legal options."
